pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-02.title: Count the bounded regions line by line
pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-02.body:
**Upper bound.** Add the lines one at a time. The $k$-th line meets the earlier lines in at most $k-1$ points, so it is cut into at most $k$ pieces: $2$ rays and at most $k-2$ finite segments. A ray splits a region into two unbounded regions, so it creates no new bounded region; each finite segment creates at most one new bounded region. Hence the number of bounded regions is at most
$$\sum_{k=2}^{14}(k-2)=0+1+\cdots+12=78.$$

**Construction.** Take $14$ lines in general position (no two parallel, no three through a point). Then the $k$-th line meets all earlier lines in $k-1$ different points and each of its $k-2$ finite segments creates a new bounded region, so there are exactly $78$ finite pieces. (Check: there are $1+14+\binom{14}2=106$ regions in all, of which $2\cdot14=28$ are unbounded, and $106-28=78$.)

**Answer: 78**

pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-03.title: Burnside's lemma
pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-03.body:
Faces of the octahedron correspond to vertices of a cube, and adjacent faces to adjacent vertices; the rotation groups are the same ($24$ rotations).

**Proper colourings (identity).** Colour the top square of the cube: a proper $3$-colouring of a $4$-cycle is either $abab$ ($6$ ways) or one pair of opposite vertices equal and the other two different ($12$ ways). For each colouring of the top, count the bottom ones (each bottom vertex must differ from the vertex above it and from its two bottom neighbours): $7$ ways after $abab$ and $6$ ways after the other type. Total $6\cdot7+12\cdot6=114$.

**Colourings fixed by each rotation.**
- $3$ half-turns about axes through opposite cube faces: top must be $abab$ ($6$ ways) and the bottom $xyxy$ with $x\ne a$, $y\ne b$, $x\ne y$ ($3$ ways): $18$ each.
- $8$ rotations of order $3$ about space diagonals: the cube vertices form orbits $\{v\},\{$3 neighbours$\}$, $\{$3 neighbours of the opposite vertex$\}$, $\{v'\}$ forming a path of colour classes: $3\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=24$ each.
- $6$ quarter-turns and $6$ half-turns about edge axes: each maps some vertex to an adjacent vertex, which forces equal colours on adjacent faces: $0$.

By Burnside the number of colourings up to rotation is
$$\frac{114+3\cdot18+8\cdot24}{24}=\frac{360}{24}=15.$$

**Answer: 15**

pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-03.title: Count by colour multiset
pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-03.body:
Let $r\ge b\ge g$ be the numbers of faces of the colours. No colour can be used on more than $4$ faces (the largest set of pairwise non-adjacent faces has $4$ elements), so the possibilities are $(4,4,0)$, $(4,3,1)$, $(4,2,2)$, $(3,3,2)$. Checking each distribution up to rotation: $(4,4,0)$ gives $1$ pattern, $(4,3,1)$ gives $1$, $(4,2,2)$ gives $1$, and $(3,3,2)$ gives $1$ (the two faces of the third colour must be opposite). Multiply by the number of ways to assign actual colours to the roles: $3$, $6$, $3$, $3$. Total $3+6+3+3=15$.

**Answer: 15**

pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-05.title: Largest antichain in a product of chains
pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-05.body:
Identify $2^x3^y5^z$ with the triple $(x,y,z)\in\{0,\dots,4\}^3$; then $p\mid q$ iff $p\le q$ coordinatewise. We want the largest antichain in this poset.

**Lower bound.** All triples with $x+y+z=6$ form an antichain (if one is coordinatewise $\le$ another with the same sum they are equal). Their number is $3,4,5,4,3$ for $x=0,1,2,3,4$ (for $x$ the pairs $(y,z)$ with $y+z=6-x$ and $y,z\le4$), i.e. $19$.

**Upper bound.** The poset is a product of chains, which has a symmetric chain decomposition (de Bruijn–Tengbergen–Kruyswijk). The number of chains equals the size of the largest rank, i.e. the number of triples with $x+y+z=6$ (the sizes of the ranks $0,\dots,12$ are $1,3,6,10,15,18,19,18,15,10,6,3,1$). Each chain contains at most one element of an antichain, so an antichain has at most $19$ elements.

**Answer: 19**

pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-06.title: Intersection points have coordinates 0, 1 or 1/2
pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-06.body:
A diagonal joins two vertices differing in a set $S$ of at least $2$ coordinates. Parametrise it by $t\in[0,1]$: the coordinates outside $S$ are constant ($0$ or $1$), and each coordinate in $S$ is $t$ or $1-t$.

**Which points occur.** Let a non-vertex point $X$ lie on two distinct diagonals $D_1$ (set $S_1$) and $D_2$ (set $S_2$). Coordinates of $X$ in $S_1$ are non-integers, but outside $S_2$ the coordinates of $D_2$ are integers, so $S_1\subseteq S_2$, and symmetrically $S_1=S_2=S$. The diagonals agree outside $S$ and are different, so some two coordinates $i,j\in S$ satisfy $x_i=x_j$ on $D_1$ but $x_i=1-x_j$ on $D_2$. At $X$ this gives $x_i=x_j=1-x_j$, so $x_i=x_j=\frac12$, hence $t=\frac12$ on $D_1$ and **all** coordinates in $S$ equal $\frac12$.

So $X$ has coordinates in $\{0,1,\frac12\}$ with at least two coordinates equal to $\frac12$.

**Each such point occurs.** Let the coordinates equal to $\frac12$ be those in $S$ ($|S|\ge2$), the others fixed values in $\{0,1\}$, and pick $i\in S$. The diagonal from ($0$ on $S$) to ($1$ on $S$) and the diagonal from ($1$ at $i$, $0$ on $S\setminus\{i\}$) to ($0$ at $i$, $1$ on $S\setminus\{i\}$) (same fixed values outside $S$) are distinct and both pass through $X$ at $t=\frac12$.

**Count.** The tuples in $\{0,1,\frac12\}^n$ with at least two entries $\frac12$ number
$$3^n-n2^{n-1}-2^n,$$
(subtract those with exactly one $\frac12$ and those with none). For $n=3$: $27-12-8=7$. For $n=5$: $243-80-32=131$.

**Answer: 131**

pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-07.title: Hall's theorem and a cyclic-shift construction
pumac-2014-combinatorics-a-07.body:
We need the smallest $k$ such that some $k$ permutations $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_k$ agree in at least one position with **every** permutation $\pi$.

**$k\le1007$ is not enough.** Build a bipartite graph between positions and numbers, joining position $i$ to number $v$ if $v\ne\sigma_j(i)$ for all $j$. Each position has at least $2014-1007=1007$ neighbours, and each number $v$ is forbidden at only $\le1007$ positions, so also has at least $1007$ neighbours. Check Hall's condition for a set $X$ of positions: if $|X|\le1007$ then $|N(X)|\ge1007\ge|X|$; if $|X|>1007$, every number has at least $1007$ neighbouring positions, more than the fewer than $1007$ positions outside $X$, so it has a neighbour in $X$ and $N(X)$ is everything. A perfect matching exists, i.e. a permutation $\pi$ that differs from every $\sigma_j$ in every position. So $1007$ papers cannot guarantee a match.

**$1008$ papers suffice.** Let paper $i$ ($1\le i\le1008$) have, in positions $1,\dots,1008$, the cyclic shift $i,i+1,\dots,1008,1,\dots,i-1$ (and anything in the other positions). For any position $p\le1008$ and any number $v\le1008$ exactly one of these papers has $v$ at position $p$. If Ding's paper has some number $v\le1008$ in some position $p\le1008$, a match exists. Otherwise the $1008$ numbers $1,\dots,1008$ would all sit in positions $1009,\dots,2014$, which has only $1006$ places: impossible.

**Answer: 1008**
